`enqueue`, `enqueue_keyed`, `enqueue_in` and cron take outbound jobs unchanged.

```rust
use charpente::kernel::JobError;
use charpente::outbound::{Call, IdempotencyKey, Reply};
use charpente::{Tx, job};

#[job(
    global,
    retain_dead,
    outbound = "pay.test",
    retry(max = 3, backoff = "1s"),
    timeout = "2s"
)]
struct Charge {
    cents: u64,
}

impl Charge {
    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
        Ok(Some(
            Call::post("/charges")
                .header("idempotency-key", key.as_str())
                .form(&[("amount", self.cents.to_string())]),
        ))
    }

    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
        match reply.status() {
            200 => Ok(()),
            s => Err(JobError::app(format!("pay.test answered {s}"))),
        }
    }
}

#[job(global, retain_dead, outbound = "mail.test")]
struct Mail {}

impl Mail {
    fn call(&self, _tx: &Tx, _key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError> {
        Ok(None)
    }

    fn settle(self, _tx: &mut Tx, _reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError> {
        Ok(())
    }
}

// One `Host` per host a mounted job calls, in any order.
use charpente::core::db::Schema;
use charpente::core::io::{Disk, Entropy};
use charpente::http::{App, AppConfig};
use charpente::jobs;
use charpente::outbound::Host;

fn build_app(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, entropy: Box<dyn Entropy>) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(disk, Schema::new(), entropy, AppConfig::default())?
        .mount_jobs(jobs![Charge, Mail])
        .outbound(Host::new("pay.test").bearer_env("PAY_KEY").max_reply_bytes(1 << 20))
        .outbound(Host::new("mail.test").header_env("X-Postmark-Server-Token", "POSTMARK_TOKEN"))
        .outbound_max_in_flight(64))
}
```

The two methods have exactly these shapes. A `global` job's:

```text
fn call(&self, tx: &Tx, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
fn settle(self, tx: &mut Tx, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
```

A `scoped_by = Org` job's take its tenant's `ScopedTx`, as its `run` would:

```text
fn call(&self, tx: &ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, key: &IdempotencyKey) -> Result<Option<Call>, JobError>
fn settle(self, tx: &mut ScopedTx<'_, '_, Org>, reply: Reply) -> Result<(), JobError>
```

`call` takes a shared `&Tx`, so it reads and cannot write: a `tx.put` inside it is
a compile error, and so is a scoped job's `call` or `settle` taking a bare `Tx`
(§9 lists both). Whatever the call's outcome should change, `settle` writes. When
there is nothing to call any more (the order was cancelled after the enqueue, say),
`call` returns `Ok(None)`, and the job is done without a call.

`key` is the job's idempotency key. The platform mints it when the job is
enqueued, 16 bytes from the node's entropy rendered as 32 lowercase hex
characters, and it stays the same across every retry and every re-dispatch after
a crash or a failover. charpente sends it nowhere by itself: `call` places it
where the remote reads one, the `idempotency-key` header above or a field of the
body, so a remote that honours it applies a repeated request once. It is not
`enqueue_keyed`'s app key.

The minted key belongs to one job and covers that job's retries and
re-dispatches. A redrive from the job's own `on_dead` hook, `tx.reissue_at` or
`tx.reissue_after` ("Re-issuing a dead job" above), resends the same request under
the same key: it copies the dead job's name, payload bytes and key, and never draws
one, so a remote that honours keys applies the effect once even if a failover
leaves one timeline re-dispatching the original while another calls the re-issue.
Any other re-issue, an effect the app enqueues again from a route, a cron tick or
another job, is a new job with a new key. So its `call` must send an id of the
effect itself, a field of the payload, or a remote that honours keys applies the
effect twice.

Because the key is drawn as the enqueue is staged, an outbound job is enqueued
only in a transaction the platform opens: a route's, a job's or a cron tick's.
`Db::transact` and `Db::begin_group` (§4) cannot mint, and a fresh outbound enqueue
inside either panics with a contract message (§9); a re-issue's key is copied from
its Dead record, not drawn, so it stages there. Code that opens its own group
stages through `Db::begin_group_minting` instead, and a test seeds an outbound job
through `App::transact_for_tests`, which the message names.

The request is built on the declared host, which is never runtime data:
`Call::get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete` take a path that begins with `/`.
`.header(name, value)` sends the name lowercase. `.json(&value)` and
`.form(&[(name, value)])` set the body and its `content-type`, and `.body(bytes)`
sets a raw body with none. A call carries one `content-type`, so setting another
(through `json`, `form` or `header`) replaces the earlier one. `settle` receives
the reply of any status, a 3xx included, since a redirect is never followed:
`reply.status()`, `reply.header(name)` (the first of that name, case-insensitively),
`reply.body()`, and `reply.json::<T>()`, which is a `JobError::App` when the body is
not `T`'s JSON.

The host is a bare DNS name like `api.stripe.com`. A scheme, port, path or
userinfo in it is a compile error, because where the host resolves is the
operator's to say. `timeout` bounds the wait for the remote's reply, with
`backoff`'s syntax; it defaults to 30 s, and it is refused on a job without
`outbound`. `cross_tenant` beside `outbound` is refused: an outbound call runs in
the one tenant its job was enqueued in. An outbound job's `impl` that has `run`
instead of `call` and `settle` fails to compile too. §9 lists each refusal's
text.

Outbound-ness is part of a job's shape: an outbound job's `FINGERPRINT` continues
its fingerprint as a pure job (`charpente::core::db::outbound_fingerprint`), so
adding `outbound` to a job, or removing it, is a shape change. It is refused while
Pending jobs of the old shape exist, and the ways through are the two "Changing a
job's fields" below describes: drain first, or a new type. The host is not part of
the shape, so changing the host is not refused.

`#[job]` writes a job's `OUTBOUND` constant and its mounted `JobDef.outbound` from
the one declaration, so the two agree. A hand-written `impl Job` or a hand-built
`JobDef` can make them disagree under the same shape, and dispatch routes a row by
whether its enqueue minted a key, so that row would reach a glue the mounted job does
not have. From `App::mount_jobs` on, such an enqueue refuses its whole transaction
before any key is drawn, and is answered the way the shape refusal in "Changing a
job's fields" below is. `<value>` is `true` or `false`, and `<declaration>` is
`a pure job` or `` `outbound = "<host>"` ``:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued with `OUTBOUND = <value>`, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — dispatch routes a row by whether its enqueue minted an idempotency key, which only an `OUTBOUND = true` enqueue does, so this row would reach a glue the mounted <job> does not have; a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
```

A row that already disagrees, enqueued by a binary that did not mount the name,
stops the kernel at dispatch with a `contract:` panic that names the job and the
fix, rather than spending its retries on a glue that cannot run.

### Declaring the hosts

An outbound job names its host; the `App` says how to reach it. Declare one
`Host` per host that a mounted job calls, as `build_app` at the end of the `Charge`
block above does.

The builders are `bearer_env(var)`, `header_env(name, var)`, `basic_env(user_var,
pass_var)`, `max_request_bytes(n)` and `max_reply_bytes(n)`. A credential is the
NAME of an environment variable. `serve` reads each value once, when it starts
(as `serve_with`, `serve_replicated`, `backup` and `archive` do, §5), and the
value never enters the log, the sim, an error text or `describe`, which lists
variable and header names only. A variable that is unset, empty, holds a
control character or is not UTF-8 refuses the start before the listener is
bound (a `basic_env` pair included, though base64 would carry a control
character: one there is a pasted newline, not a credential). The one
exception is a `basic_env` password, which may be empty, since APIs that take
the key as the username (Stripe's `-u sk_…:`) send `user:`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
outbound: <var> is unset — host <host> needs it for job <job>
outbound: <var> is set but empty — host <host> needs it for job <job>
outbound: <var> holds a control character (a trailing newline, say) or is not UTF-8 — host <host> needs it for job <job>; set it to the credential alone
```

`<job>` is the first mounted job that calls `<host>`. The caps default to
1 MiB and 4 MiB, and neither passes `MAX_CAP_BYTES` (8 MiB).

Each host is reached at `https://<host>:443` over HTTP/1.1, its certificate
verified against Mozilla's root store (`webpki-roots`, so the answer does not
vary with the machine's OS). An operator moves the address with
`--outbound-base` and adds a CA with `--outbound-ca` (§5); neither changes the
name that TLS verifies. No redirect is followed, so a 3xx is a reply that
`settle` reads. The client neither retries nor times out on its own: both are
the kernel's, through `retry` and `timeout`.

The two sets must match both ways, checked when the kernel is built, so mount
order is free. A called host with no entry is refused with
`kernel: job <job> calls <host>, which has no Host entry — add
app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) with the credentials it needs (GUIDE §6)`,
and an entry no mounted job calls with `kernel:
app.outbound(Host::new("<host>")) declares a host no mounted job calls —
remove it, or mount the job that calls it`. Declaring one host twice panics
at `app.outbound`. `app.outbound_hosts()` returns the hosts the mounted jobs
call, sorted: the list `sim.outbound` takes.

`app.outbound_max_in_flight(n)` sets how many calls a node keeps in flight at
once (default 64, `charpente::outbound::DEFAULT_MAX_IN_FLIGHT`). A due
outbound job waits while the table is full, and a pure job never waits behind
it.

### When a call fails

The kernel starts a call only after the transaction that ran `call` has
committed, so a call never goes out on state that did not become durable,
including a write by another job in the same batch that `call` read. It waits
for the reply outside any transaction, for at most `timeout`, and hands the
reply to `settle`. An attempt below counts against `retry` the way a failed
`run` does: `attempts` increments, `last_error` names the failure, and the job
waits out its backoff or goes Dead, running its `on_dead` hook if it declares one
("What a job's Dead means" above). Every retry carries the job's key unchanged.

| What happens | An attempt? | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `call` returns `Ok(None)` | — | Done; no call |
| `call` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`call panicked: …`) | yes | failure record; no call |
| `call` builds a request its `Host` entry refuses | yes | failure record naming the rule; no call |
| `call` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles: restart-and-recover |
| a transport failure: refused, TLS, DNS, a reset, a reply over the cap | yes | failure record |
| `timeout` passes with no reply | yes | the call is cancelled; failure record |
| a reply for a call that already timed out or was dropped | — | discarded, counted in `outbound_late` |
| `settle` returns `Ok` | — | its writes and the Done mark commit as one record |
| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::App)` or panics (`settle panicked: …`) | yes | its writes discarded; failure record |
| `settle` returns `Err(JobError::Io)` | no | bubbles; still Pending, called again after the restart |
| the process crashes with calls in flight | no | the Pending jobs are called again on restart |
| the node stops being writable (a switchover, a demotion) | no | its calls in flight are dropped; the next writable node calls again |
| the node is restored from its archive | no | Pending rows keep their key, so a re-call is the same request |

An attempt that may have reached the remote says so. Only a refused connection
certainly did not, so it is the one text that says the call never arrived:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
outbound <host>: <error> — the call did not reach the remote
outbound <host>: <error> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
outbound <host>: timed out after <timeout> — the remote may have applied this call; the retry carries the same idempotency key
outbound <host>: the reply exceeded the <cap>-byte reply cap — the remote answered, so it applied this call; raise the cap with Host::max_reply_bytes (the retry carries the same idempotency key)
```

The first line is a call whose connection never opened, so no byte of it was
sent: a refused connection, a failed DNS lookup or a failed TLS handshake. Its
`<error>` names which: `connection refused` in the sim, and in production
`could not connect: ` and the client's cause chain (`client error (Connect):
tcp connect error: Connection refused (os error 61)`, say), or `the outbound
runtime thread is gone` for a call the client's dead thread never took. The second is
every other transport failure's. `<timeout>` is the
job's `timeout` as Rust prints a `Duration` (`2s`, `1.5s`), and `<cap>` is the
host's reply cap in bytes.

**Dead means no reply was settled.** It does not mean nothing happened at the
remote: a call whose reply was lost, or that timed out, may have been applied
there. The Dead job's `last_error` says which of the texts above ended it.

**A remote that ignores the key is called again, and may bill again.** A retry
after a lost reply or a timeout sends the same request with the same key. A
remote with Stripe's semantics applies it once. Many remotes do not dedupe at
all, LLM APIs among them, so a lost reply there means a second completion is
requested and paid for. `settle` still commits at most once, so the app's state
stays exactly-once, but the remote's bill does not.

**A crash-looping process calls again on every restart.** A crash is not an
attempt, as `JobError::Io` is not, so it spends nothing from `retry`. A job
whose dispatch keeps killing the process is called again each time it comes
back, without end.

**Deploying a changed `call` under a key in flight.** A call in flight when the
process stops is called again by whichever binary comes up next. If that
binary's `call` builds different parameters, the remote receives the old key
with new parameters. Stripe-style APIs refuse that (the sim's `Idempotent`
model answers 409, §8), and `settle` receives the refusal as an ordinary reply.
Change what `call` sends the way "Changing a job's fields" below changes a
job's shape: drain the type's Pending jobs on the old binary first, or send the
new request from a new job type.

**In a sim test.** A kernel over an app that mounts an outbound job needs an
`Outbound`, and every constructor refuses to build without one:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
kernel: job <job> calls <host>, but this kernel has no Outbound — serve() supplies the production client; a sim test passes one: let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?; Kernel::with_outbound(app, clock, Box::new(outbound))
```

Register a model for each host with `sim.remote` (§8), then build the handle
from the app before the kernel takes it:

```rust
use charpente::http::App;
use charpente::kernel::{Kernel, SimSource};
use charpente_sim::Sim;

fn run_with_outbound(sim: &Sim, app: App, horizon_nanos: u64) -> std::io::Result<Kernel> {
    let outbound = sim.outbound(&app.outbound_hosts())?;
    let mut kernel = Kernel::with_outbound(app, Box::new(sim.clock()), Box::new(outbound))?;
    kernel.run(&mut SimSource::new(Box::new(sim.clock()), horizon_nanos))?;
    Ok(kernel)
}
```

A node that also replicates or archives is built with `Kernel::builder(app,
clock)`, then any of `.replication(repl)`, `.archive(archive, store)` and
`.outbound(outbound)`, then `.build()`. `kernel.stats()` counts the arm's work
in `outbound_started` (calls started), `outbound_settled` (replies whose
`settle` committed), `outbound_failed` (every failure record: a failed or
refused `call`, a transport failure, a timeout, a failed `settle`),
`outbound_timed_out` and `outbound_late` (replies discarded, including any
still buffered when the node stopped being writable).

### Changing a job's fields

Every enqueue records the payload's shape — `Job::FINGERPRINT`, the structural
fingerprint `#[job]` computes from the fields (§12) — and a Pending job is only ever
decoded by a binary that compiled that same shape. A node about to become able to
dispatch refuses while any Pending job of a type it mounts was enqueued under another
shape. It checks at startup and at every moment its write gate opens (a witness gate
opening, a completed switchover), and `promote` checks before it changes anything:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) were enqueued under a different shape of <job> (recorded <recorded>; this binary <fingerprint>) — this binary will not decode them; run the binary that enqueued them until they are Done or Dead, then deploy this one, or restore whichever of <job>'s fields, its `global`/`scoped_by` declaration, its `outbound` declaration or its tenant type's `NAME` changed, and give the new shape its own #[job] type under a new name (GUIDE §6)
```

A job's tenancy is part of its shape. A `scoped_by` job's fingerprint continues its
fields' fold over its tenant type's `NAME` (§16), so moving a job between `global` and
`scoped_by`, or to a tenant type with another `NAME`, is refused the same way. A deploy
therefore never hands a row enqueued with no tenant to a scoped `run`, one enqueued in a
tenant to a global one, or one enqueued in a tenant of one `NAME` to a job of another.
Respelling the `scoped_by` path is not a shape change while it names a type of the same
`NAME`: see below, after the scope-type refusal, for what that leaves unchecked.

At most five ids are listed, then `…`. A job enqueued before shapes were recorded reads
`recorded none — enqueued before job shapes were tagged`, and it is refused the same way:
nothing decodes bytes it cannot prove are its own shape.

- At startup, or when the write gate opens, the refusal stops the kernel, and a stopped
  kernel ends the process (§5).
- At `promote`, it answers `CtrlErr` prefixed `cannot promote:`, and the node stays a
  follower.
- A switchover is never refused partway. Once the old primary hands off it never resumes
  on its own (DESIGN §5 calls the hand-off its point of no return), so a refusal there
  would leave neither node writable. The switchover completes. The new primary's kernel
  then stops at the moment it becomes writable, with the refusal above, and its fix works
  from there: run the binary that enqueued the jobs on that node, now the primary, until
  they are Done or Dead. The old primary follows it throughout.

Done and Dead rows are never decoded again and never refuse anything. A Pending row of a
job type this binary does not mount keeps the "not registered" path above.

This binary never writes a foreign-shape row itself. `NAME` is the type's bare identifier,
so two `#[job]` types can share one: a route that still enqueues `v1::SendReceipt` in a
binary that mounts `v2::SendReceipt`, say. From `App::mount_jobs` on — whether or not a
kernel exists yet — an enqueue under another shape of a mounted name refuses its whole
transaction before anything is written:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued under a different shape of <job> than this binary mounts (enqueued <shape>; this binary <fingerprint>) — two #[job] types share the name <job>; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, or give the other type its own name (GUIDE §6)
```

A route answers it with a 500 carrying that text, never the retryable storage-failure 500
(§5). Inside a job handler it is an attempt, like a panic: the job retries and then
dead-letters, with the text as its `last_error`. In a cron schedule's enqueue it stops the
kernel. An enqueue of a job type this binary does not mount at all is not refused here: it
commits and takes the "not registered" path.

Tenancy has a twin of both refusals. `#[job]` fingerprints `scoped_by`, but a
hand-written `impl Job` can copy a mounted job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under the other
tenancy, and a hand-written `JobDef` can mount a job under the wrong one. Either would
hand the dispatcher a row with a tenant for a `global` job, or with none for a `scoped_by`
one. So an enqueue whose tenant presence disagrees with the mounted declaration refuses
its transaction the same way, and a Pending row that already disagrees is refused
wherever the shape refusal runs. `<presence>` is `a tenant` or `no tenant`, and
`<declaration>` is `` `global` `` or `` `scoped_by = Org` ``:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued with <presence>, but this binary mounts <job> as <declaration> under the same shape (<shape>) — a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef` contradicts <job>'s #[job]; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted type, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
<n> Pending "<job>" job(s) (ids <ids>) carry <presence>, but this binary declares <job> <declaration> — the enqueue family writes a tenant exactly for a `scoped_by` job, so something that contradicts <job>'s #[job] wrote these rows: a hand-written `impl Job` or `JobDef`, or a raw store write; this binary will not dispatch them; mount <job> as its #[job] declares it, or restore the store from a replica or backup taken before these rows were written. For a follower, or a primary once a follower is promoted in its place, that is a re-seed: stop the node, delete its data dir, and restart it configured as a follower of the current primary so it snapshot-seeds from it, never with a primary config: the durable role file that outranks config is deleted with the data dir, so a cleared node started as a primary comes up as a second writable primary (GUIDE §6)
```

Presence is not the whole of a tenant. A row records the tenant's id and not the scope type
it is an id of, and the dispatcher opens that id as the type the mounted job declares. The
fingerprint tells two scope types apart only by their `NAME`s. A `#[job(scoped_by = Desk)]`
in a module that says `use super::Board as Desk;` fingerprints with `Board`'s `NAME`, so it
is refused as another shape. But a `#[job]` whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type
with the same `NAME` fingerprints alike, and a hand-written `impl Job` can copy both
constants under any `type Scope`. Enqueued inside a tenant of that other type, either would
run the mounted job in the same id of the type it declares, a tenant nothing opened or
named for it. So an
enqueue whose job's scope type is not the one the mounted job declares refuses its
transaction the same way. `<scope>` is the enqueuing job's tenant type's `NAME` and `<declared>` the
mounted one's (§16); `<id>` is the tenant id. The two NAMEs can be equal. A hand-built `JobDef` that
names one type and carries another's `scope_type` is refused here on the honest enqueue, which is why
the text says "with another scope type" and lists that cause:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
job "<job>" was enqueued in a `<scope>` tenant, but this binary mounts <job> as `scoped_by = <declared>` with another scope type under the same shape (<shape>) — a job row records its tenant's id and not its type, so tenant <id> would be read as the mounted declaration's type, not the one it was enqueued in; either a type standing in for <job>'s #[job] was enqueued (a hand-written `impl Job`, or a #[job] whose `scoped_by` names another tenant type with the same `NAME`), or a hand-written `JobDef` mounts <job> under a `scope_type` its #[job] does not declare; the transaction was refused and nothing was written, so a retry cannot succeed — enqueue the mounted <job> from a `<declared>` scope, give the other type its own name, or mount <job> as its #[job] declares it (GUIDE §6)
```

One door is left inside a binary, and it is a hand-built `JobDef`. Its fields are public,
so `JobDef { glue: <another job's glue>, ..<File as JobEntry>::def() }` mounts a glue that
opens a different scope type than `scope_type` names, and so does a `JobDef` whose
`scoped_by` and `scope_type` both name a type its glue does not open. `Group::stage` holds
the enqueuer to `scope_type`, and a scoped job's glue opens its row's tenant through
`JobScope::open`, which asserts that the type it opens is `scope_type`. The assert runs
inside the attempt, so the job retries and then dead-letters, and nothing runs in either
tenant. Its `last_error`, for `File`'s `JobDef` carrying a `Board` job's glue, is below.
`<path>` is `Board`'s `std::any::type_name`, printed beside its `NAME` so that a glue whose
type shares the declared `NAME` still reads as two types:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
handler panicked: contract: the glue mounted for job "File" opened its tenant 31 as `Board` (the tenant type `<path>`), but that `JobDef` declares `scoped_by = Desk` with a `scope_type` that is not `<path>` — a hand-built `JobDef` whose `glue` or `scope_type` disagrees with its #[job] (a glue taken from another job, or another type's `TypeId`); this attempt wrote nothing, and every retry fails the same way — mount File through `jobs![…]`, which builds its `JobDef` from its #[job] (GUIDE §6)
```

A `JobDef` whose glue and `scope_type` name the same other type passes the assert. Nothing
can tell it apart, and it does not cross a tenant: `Group::stage` held the enqueuer to
that same type, so the job runs in the tenant it was enqueued in, only with another job's
code. `jobs![…]` builds every `JobDef` from its `#[job]`, and it is the way to mount one.

This one has no startup twin, because a row carries no type to compare, only the `NAME`
its fingerprint mixes. The check runs where both types are known, at the enqueue, in a
binary that mounts the job. At startup the dispatching binary compares a Pending row's
shape, so a row whose job named a tenant type of another `NAME` is refused there by the
foreign-shape refusal above. That covers the refactor that turns a job module's `use
billing::Org;` into `use crm::Org;`, whenever the two types' NAMEs differ. What a later
binary that mounts the name dispatches unchecked, in the scope type it declares, is a row
whose shape matches:

- a row a hand-written `impl Job` enqueued from a binary that did not mount the job name,
  copying the job's `NAME` and `FINGERPRINT` under another `type Scope`;
- a row enqueued under a tenant type with the same `NAME` as the mounted one. A `NAME` is
  the tenant's identity, so this is the same tenant by declaration: giving a type another
  type's `NAME` declares it that tenant, and one app cannot mount both (§16).

Where the recorded shape matches the mounted one, neither is refused, at startup or at
dispatch. So before a deploy that mounts a scoped job the running binary does not mount,
drain that job: run the binary that enqueued its Pending rows until every one is Done or
Dead, the first way through a shape change below.

There are two ways through a shape change:

- **Drain first.** Run the binary that enqueued them — the old one after an upgrade, the
  newer one after a rollback — until every Pending job of the type is Done or Dead (each
  reaches one within its retry policy), then deploy. In a replicated pair, drain on the
  primary before a switchover onto a follower running another shape, or that follower
  stops as described above.
- **A new type.** Leave the old type's fields alone, put the new fields in a new `#[job]`
  type under a new name, mount both, and switch enqueues to the new one. The name is not
  optional: `NAME` is the type's own identifier, and `mount_jobs` panics on two jobs of
  one name. The old type keeps dispatching its rows, because their shape is still its
  own; remove it once none are Pending.

What the fingerprint cannot see, a change inside a type a field holds, is in §12.

### What `#[job]` rejects

Every rejection is a compile error naming the contract and the fix. The first is the
one every job meets once, and the next three are its neighbours:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` declares no tenancy — a job says which. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `scoped_by = Org` if it acts inside one tenant (it is enqueued from inside that tenant's scope, and its `run` receives that tenant's `ScopedTx`), or `global` if it belongs to no tenant (the only kind cron can schedule). Neither is the default.
`global` and `scoped_by = <scope>` on one job — a job is one or the other; drop one
`global` given twice — write it once
`scoped_by` given twice — write it once
```

The second every job meets once too, right after the first: a job that names its
tenancy and not what its Dead means ("What a job's Dead means" above). Its
neighbours refuse both stances at once and either one twice:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` declares no Dead stance — a job says what its Dead means. Add one of these to its `#[job(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `on_dead` if the app must act when the job's retries run out (the job then has `fn on_dead(self, tx: &mut Tx, dead: Dead<Self>) -> Result<(), JobError>`, whose writes commit with the Dead mark), or `retain_dead` if the Dead row, kept with its last error, is all that should happen. Neither is the default.
`on_dead` and `retain_dead` are two answers to one question — keep the one this job means
`on_dead` given twice — write it once
`retain_dead` given twice — write it once
```

A `scoped_by` job enqueued where no tenant is named — `tx.enqueue` on a bare `Tx`, or
`App::schedule` — is an unsatisfied bound, and rustc prints this note with your job and
scope in place of `<job>` and `<scope>` (§16 shows it rendered):

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<job>` is a tenant-scoped job (`#[job(scoped_by = <scope>)]`) and a bare `Tx` names no tenant to run it in
enqueue it from inside the tenant it acts in, and it runs in that tenant:
    let mut tx = tx.scope::<<scope>>(scope, ctx)?;
    tx.enqueue(job);
or fan it out from a `cross_tenant` route or job, naming the tenant:
    tx.enqueue_in::<<scope>>(scope, job, cap);
cron (`App::schedule`) enqueues on a bare `Tx`, so it schedules `global` jobs only
```

The rest are about the attribute's syntax and the struct's shape:

```rust,ignore
// a word the attribute does not recognise
#[job(bogus)]
struct Foo {}
// "a job declares `global` or `scoped_by = <Type>` and one of `on_dead` /
//  `retain_dead`, and may add `cross_tenant`, `retry(max = <int>, backoff =
//  \"<n><unit>\")` (unit is one of ms, s, m, h), and `outbound = \"<host>\"`
//  with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in any order — e.g.
//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = \"10s\"))]`,
//  `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead,
//  outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout = \"30s\")]`"

// backoff with no unit suffix
#[job(global, retain_dead, retry(max = 3, backoff = "10"))]
struct Bar {}
// "backoff \"10\" has no unit — a job declares `global` or `scoped_by =
//  <Type>` and one of `on_dead` / `retain_dead`, and may add `cross_tenant`,
//  `retry(max = <int>, backoff = \"<n><unit>\")` (unit is one of ms, s, m, h),
//  and `outbound = \"<host>\"` with an optional `timeout = \"<n><unit>\"`, in
//  any order — e.g. `#[job(scoped_by = Org, retain_dead, retry(max = 3,
//  backoff = \"10s\"))]`, `#[job(global, cross_tenant, on_dead)]` or
//  `#[job(scoped_by = Org, on_dead, outbound = \"api.stripe.com\", timeout =
//  \"30s\")]`"

// enums and unions cannot be job payloads
#[job(global, retain_dead)]
enum Baz {
    A,
}
// "#[job] applies to structs — enums and unions cannot be job payloads"
```

## 7. Cron

Cron rides the same kernel loop as HTTP requests and jobs (§5, §6) — a
schedule is a row, and a due tick is one transaction that advances the
schedule and enqueues a job through the exact same path `tx.enqueue` uses:
a recurring enqueuer, inheriting retry and observability for free.

133	### Drawing inputs
134	
135	`sim.input()` is for the inputs a property must hold for: a name, an amount, an
136	order of operations. Each draw comes from a stream of its own, so drawing moves
137	no fault, and the harness records each draw's choice in a sequence it can replay
138	and shrink. The choice is the one the draw used: the stream's raw value reduced
139	into the draw's range, which is the smallest raw value that draws the same
140	value. So a choice and its value are one to one, and two equal values drawn
141	with the same bounds are equal choices.
142	
143	```text
144	let i = sim.input();
145	let qty = i.between("qty", 1, 500);        // inclusive; shrinks toward 1
146	let kind = i.pick("kind", &["a", "b"]);    // shrinks toward the first item
147	i.shuffle("order", &mut ops);              // shrinks toward the given order
148	let note = i.text("note", &["x", "y"], 1, 4);
149	```
150	
151	It is the workload's own script only: a modelled remote keeps its own `Rng`. A
152	drawn input tests how the app handles what its model stand-in returns, never
153	the real model's behaviour. `between` panics when `lo > hi`, and `pick` on an
154	empty slice. `text` panics when `min_words > max_words`, and on an empty
155	`words` when `max_words` is above 0; with a `max_words` of 0 it draws `""`.
156	Each message names the call and the draw, and says which argument to change.
157	
158	When a check fails, its first failure is shrunk to smaller draws that still
159	fail it, and the failure block lists them by name on its `inputs:` line
160	("Shrinking a failure" below).
161	
162	A loop's length decides how well it shrinks. When the length is a drawn count
163	(`let n = i.between("notes", 1, 4);` and then `n` items, the shape of the
164	scaffold's `tests/sim.rs` and `drawn_inputs.rs`), deleting one item leaves the
165	count stale: the loop reads the next item's draws in its place, the draws after
166	the loop shift, and the run usually passes, while lowering the count alone
167	drops the last item instead. So the shrink can keep items a smaller count would
168	drop. The failure still replays and is still the failure it was, but the shrunk
169	run may not be minimal. When the items after the first matter to a failure (a
170	later item, or a draw after the loop, depends on them), draw a "one more?"
171	choice before each item instead, so that deleting an item deletes exactly its
172	draws:

175	let mut qtys = Vec::new();
176	while qtys.len() < 6 && *i.pick("more", &[false, true]) {  // shrinks toward stopping
177	    qtys.push(i.between("qty", 1, 500));
178	}
179	```

182	drew: two runs that drew the same values, under the same names and in the same
183	order, count once.
184	It is a count, never a threshold. A check whose workload draws nothing is named
185	above the check lines, because every one of its runs tested the same scripted
186	case, whatever the faults did ("Reading a batch" below).

188	### Giving up: a skipped run
189	
190	Sooner or later a workload hits a run where the faults are severe enough
191	that it cannot test its claim at all: the database never opened, the write was
192	never acknowledged, every recovery attempt was exhausted, or durable corruption
193	cut the very record the claim was about. That is not a pass —
194	nothing was proven — and it is not a failure either; the harness did exactly
195	what it was told.
196	
197	Say so:

204	#[table(global)]
205	struct Counter {
206	    id: Id<Counter>,
207	    hits: u64,
208	}

210	fn counter_survives(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
211	    let schema = || Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
212	    // A boot that meets an injected fault restarts and boots again, as a
213	    // supervised process would: `Db::open`'s contract for an IO failure.
214	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
215	    let Some(mut db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
216	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
217	    else {
218	        // Nothing to adjudicate: the disk never let the claim become testable.
219	        sim.give_up("Db::open never booted in 8 boots", "");
220	        return Ok(());
221	    };

224	            id: Id::from_raw(1),
225	            hits: 1,
226	        });

228	    });

230	        Ok(()) => {}

232	        // Any other error is the platform's, and fails, as the opens do.

234	            sim.give_up("the write was never acknowledged, so there is no claim to check", e);
235	            return Ok(());
236	        }
237	        Err(e) => return Err(format!("{e:?}")),
238	    }

253	        // needs a verdict.
254	        Ok(None) if durable_corruption_fired(sim) => {
255	            sim.give_up("durable corruption cut the acked row, so durability was not adjudicated", "");
256	            Ok(())
257	        }
258	        Ok(None) => Err("acked Counter row lost across a crash".to_string()),
259	        Err(e) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => {

268	- `sim.give_up(reason, detail)` records the give-up **on the run**, not in
269	  the value you return. That is deliberate: a `Result` can be mapped back to
270	  `Ok(())` by a wrapper before the runner ever sees it, and for a long time
271	  that is exactly what happened — a property could report green having
272	  concluded nothing over most of its runs.
273	- **The reason is fixed text; the detail is this run's own.** `reason` is a
274	  `&'static str` that names the *kind* of give-up and embeds nothing that
275	  varies between runs: no error text, count or seq. A batch groups each
276	  check's skipped runs by reason and counts each group, so a reason with a seq
277	  in it makes every run its own group and the counts say nothing. What varies
278	  goes in `detail` (anything `Display`, such as the fallout error `e`): that one
279	  run's own text, which a batch does not print and `--seed` prints under the
280	  skipped check as `detail:`. A batch gives each reason the seed of its first
281	  run, `(first: --seed 0x…)`, so `charpente test --sim --filter <check> --seed
282	  0x…` replays that run and prints its detail, then a `fired:` line: what
283	  fired in that run, rendered as a failure block's `fired:` line is (less its
284	  own `run:skipped`), the line to reason from about why it gave up. A
285	  constant such as a retry count is fixed text, so it belongs in the reason
286	  (`"Db::open never booted in 8 boots"`), not the detail. A give-up with
287	  nothing to add passes `""`, and an empty detail is none.
288	  `sim.gave_up()` reads the reason and `sim.gave_up_detail()` the detail;
289	  `Outcome::GaveUp` carries both.
290	- First call wins, reason and detail together; later ones are consequences of
291	  the first.
292	- **Give up and stop.** The record is sticky and nothing enforces terminality,
293	  so if you give up inside a retry arm and the loop then goes on to adjudicate,
294	  the run is still reported as skipped and that verdict is thrown away.
295	  `give_up` and the `return`/`break` belong on the same arm. This bites hardest
296	  in a multi-round checker on your own `sim` (`acked_implies_durable`).
297	- A workload that gives up and then returns `Err` is still a **failure**.
298	  Failures outrank give-ups.
299	- It also marks the coverage key `run:skipped` — once per run, not
300	  once per call — so a give-up *rate* is counted like any other sometimes-key,
301	  and it cross-checks the reported count exactly. A run that gives up and
302	  then returns `Err` is counted as failed, so `charpente test --sim` counts
303	  every key it reached, toward `require` and in the JSON's `coverage`, except
304	  its `run:skipped`. `ceiling:
305	  [("run:skipped", N)]` on `run_universes_swarm!`/`run_universes_swarm_with!`
306	  caps it: the batch fails when more than N runs gave up, naming the key,
307	  the count and the cap. Twenty of the platform's own swarm properties carry
308	  one:
309	  - kernel's exactly-once and job-tenancy properties;
310	  - the flagship properties of tenant, transactions, http, group_commit and
311	    typed_tables, and archive's two convergence properties;
312	  - realtime's flagship, scoped settled-client and tenant-feed properties,
313	    migrations' two, and the WAL suite's fault-matrix, bit-flip, misdirected-write, read-error,
314	    dir-entry and gc properties.
315	
316	  The rest carry none yet, so a drift in their give-up rates is visible only in
317	  the split: realtime's mixed-shapes and follower properties, replication's,
318	  auth's, kernel's job-shape property, transactions' crashed-reseed property,
319	  and engine's. A give-up is
320	  reported and never failed, so without a cap a property can drift toward
321	  adjudicating nothing with every batch green; a floor on the key would bound
322	  give-ups from below, which guards nothing. An app's `sim_tests!` takes no
323	  `ceiling:`. Its property `require`s instead the key its verdict marks, past
324	  every give-up arm. That fails a batch in which no run reached a verdict,
325	  but not one whose rate merely drifted.
326	- A cap bounds what a property fails to conclude, not how much it checks, so
327	  pair it with a `floor: [("key", N)]` on the key that counts its checks
328	  (written before `ceiling:`, on either macro). A change that skips a round's
329	  work without giving up meets every cap. At a pinned base the floor is the
330	  exact count; at an ambient one it is a margin, the mean over ten or more
331	  fresh batches less four standard deviations (§8).
332	- If your workload already funnels give-ups through a wrapper (the
333	  `Err("universe-inconclusive: …")` idiom the platform's own suites use), put
334	  the `sim.give_up(INCONCLUSIVE, e)` call there, beside the `sim.cover(...)` mark. Keep
335	  both: the coverage keys are a floorable distribution over *causes*, and the
336	  outcome is the scalar the runner reports. Neither replaces the other.
337	
338	Every batch states, check by check, how many runs tested the check and, when any
339	were skipped, how many and why. A check with nothing skipped shows no skipped
340	count and is left out of the reasons block, and a batch that skipped nothing
341	prints no reasons block at all. This is a pinned batch of `crates/sim-fixture`,
342	`charpente test --sim --runs 64 --master-seed 0x5eed --filter counter_roundtrip`:

373	skipped runs hit a fault before reaching the check, so they prove nothing either way:
374	  always_gives_up — never tested: every run was skipped
375	    6  the fixture always gives up (first: --seed 0x3071c63893f2dcbd)
376	a check that tested nothing proves nothing, so the batch fails: the reasons above say where its runs stopped. Raise --runs, change the setup until runs reach the check (charpente_sim::drive runs the faulted phase, the recovery and the re-sends), or delete the check.
377	
378	these checks draw no inputs, so every run tested the same case — draw them with sim.input() (GUIDE §8):
379	  always_passes
380	
381	check always_passes ..... ok  (6 tested)
382	check always_gives_up ... untested  (0 tested, 6 skipped)
383	
384	sim result: FAILED. 1 passed; 0 failed; 1 untested. Runs tested per check, in the order above: 6, 0 of 6.
385	rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x1234 --runs 6
386	```
387	
388	"Reading a batch" below describes each line.
389	
390	**Where the split is visible, and where it is not.** `charpente test --sim`
391	always prints it: the sim binary is `harness = false`, so nothing captures its
392	output. The platform's own internal suites print a line of their own —
393	
394	```text
395	charpente-sim [replication]: 38 of 128 universes reached a verdict, 90 gave up
396	```
397	
398	— but that one goes to stderr from inside a libtest `#[test]`, so **a passing
399	`cargo test` swallows it.** Add `-- --nocapture` to see it (a failing test
400	shows it either way). So do not expect a CI run to surface give-ups; go
401	looking for them. The one exception is a test in which every universe gave up,
402	which fails, as an untested check fails a batch:
403	
404	```text
405	charpente-sim [wal]: every universe gave up, so this test adjudicated nothing over 64 universes and fails. Raise its universe count, or change the workload until universes reach a verdict.
406	```
407	
408	A `CHARPENTE_SEED` replay of one universe that gave up still passes, as a
409	`--seed` replay of a skipped run exits 0.
410	
411	Read that example line the right way round: **38** of those 128 runs
412	adjudicated the property and **90** did not. It is a real measurement from
413	`wal_corruption_on_the_primary_no_longer_loses_acked_records_with_a_follower`,
414	and it means 70% of that property's runs prove nothing — which was
415	invisible before the split was printed, and is the entire reason it is.
416	
417	### A fault-free tail for an end-of-run check
418	
419	A recovery under faults is four steps, and `charpente_sim::drive` runs them.
420	The app supplies how it builds itself on the run's sim and what to send;
421	"Driving the whole app in a sim" below has a compiled workload built on it.
422	
423	```text
424	let drive = Drive::new(sim, build_app); // build_app: Fn(&Sim) -> io::Result<App>
425	let phase = drive.faulted_phase(&requests, Duration::from_secs(2))?; // steps 1 and 2
426	calm.store(true, Ordering::Relaxed); // a remote model's own switch stays yours
427	let Some(recovered) = drive.recover(&phase, Duration::from_secs(60))? else {
428	    return Ok(()); // given up by name
429	}; // steps 3 and 4
430	let snap = recovered.kernel.app().db().snapshot().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
431	```
432	
433	1. **Boot through fallout.** `faulted_phase` boots the app with
434	   `boot_through_fallout` (below), up to eight boots, restarting between
435	   them as a supervisor would. A first boot that never gets past fault
436	   fallout is no give-up: the phase is empty, and `recover` sends
437	   everything. In every step, fault fallout means `is_fault_fallout(t) ||
438	   clock_fallout(sim, t)`.
439	2. **A faulted phase.** The requests, each an offset from the instant the app
440	   booted and in arrival order, run through one kernel under the run's faults
441	   until nothing is left inside the horizon. An offset past the horizon
442	   panics before anything runs, since the phase would never send that
443	   request, naming the last offset, the horizon and the fix: raise the
444	   horizon past the last request, or space the requests closer. An offset
445	   equal to the horizon is sent. The kernel gets the sim's
446	   outbound handle exactly when the app declares hosts. Fault fallout ends
447	   the phase: it is the crash under test, never a give-up and never a skip,
448	   and the answers already recorded stand. `phase.answers[i]` is request
449	   `i`'s `(status, body)`, or `None` when it went unanswered;
450	   `phase.status(i)` is its status.
451	3. **A tail free of per-call faults; a drawn provider outage runs to its
452	   end.** `recover` power-cycles (`sim.restart()`), quiesces the disk and
453	   clock faults, and the outbound faults when the app declares hosts. A drawn
454	   `outbound_outage` is not a roll, so it refuses its host until its own end.
455	   It waits out a clock refusal, boots, and runs the kernel to `tail` past the
456	   instant it booted, so due jobs, retries and cron drain, then on until the
457	   app's outbound work settles (below). A remote model's own switches, such
458	   as `modelled_remote`'s `calm`, stay in your code: flip them between the two
459	   calls.
460	4. **Re-send what went unanswered.** Every request whose answer is `None`,
461	   or a 5xx whose body is fault fallout, is sent again at the tail's start. A
462	   4xx, or a handler's own 5xx, is the app's answer and is not re-sent.
463	   Fallout is read from the body's text (`is_fault_fallout`), so a handler's
464	   own 5xx whose message reads as fallout ("injected", say) is re-sent too.
465	   The re-sent answers come back in `recovered.resent`, apart from the
466	   phase's, because a request that went unanswered may or may not have
467	   landed. So a claim about acked requests reads `phase.status(i) ==
468	   Some(200)`, and a check that wants the two merged merges them itself
469	   (`examples/drawn_inputs.rs`). A re-sent request lands after everything the
470	   faulted phase ran, not at its offset, so work its offset came before may
471	   already have run by then: a cancel drawn ahead of a reminder's due time
472	   that went unanswered can land after the reminder was sent. A check that
473	   judges when a request took effect treats a re-sent one (a `Some` in
474	   `recovered.resent`) as landing after the phase, since `Recovered` gives no
475	   instant for the tail's start.
476	
477	**The tail settles outbound work.** After the run to `tail`, `recover` reads
478	the store and the wall time the kernel judges due times by: the greater of the
479	clock's reading and the kernel's held wall, which the kernel's open seeds from
480	the store's recorded time, so it can sit up to the 60 s clock tolerance above
481	the clock. It stops when every Pending outbound row is not yet due: no attempt
482	made, and a due time after that wall time, as a delayed job (§6) or a re-issue
483	scheduled later is. Any other Pending outbound row extends the tail: the
484	kernel runs again, as far as the most, over those rows, of the row's wait (to
485	its due time; none once it is due) or the drawn outage's remaining length,
486	whichever is longer, plus its job's declared timeout plus 1 s, and the store
487	is read again. Idle virtual time costs a wake-up, so a retry's wait costs at
488	most one extension and so does a drawn outage, however long: through a 4 h
489	outage a `retry(max = 12)` job takes two extensions, not 17 hours of work, and
490	no app sizes `tail` to its retry policy. An `on_dead` hook that enqueues a fresh job
491	on every Dead, or re-issues at once, makes a chain that ends when the outage
492	ends: through a 4 h outage two such chains on the default policy take one
493	extension, and one on `crates/outbound-fixture`'s `ChargeOrder` policy (eight
494	attempts in 63.5 s) takes two. The extensions stop at
495	`charpente_sim::drive::TAIL_SETTLE_CAP`, 256, with work still Pending, and the
496	run fails by name (below). No extension runs past the year 2262: a retry whose
497	doubling backoff grew past it stays Pending, and once one extension has run to
498	that limit the run fails at once, by its own text naming the job's due time
499	(below), rather than at the end of the u64 nanosecond range, where the kernel
500	stops on its daily sweep's overflow. An app with no host has no outbound row,
501	so it is never extended. `recovered.extensions` counts the extensions, and
502	`recovered.wall` is the wall time the tail stopped at, the time to pass
503	`outbound_settles_by_horizon` ("The checkers", below).
504	
505	**Coverage for a Dead path.** Last, `recover` calls `mark_dead_coverage`
506	("The checkers"), which marks `dead:<job>` once per Dead row, whatever the
507	job's stance: `dead:SendReceipt` for a `SendReceipt` job. Require it to hold
508	that the job's Dead path ran, as `crates/outbound-fixture`'s sim does:
509	`orders_charge_once require ["outbound:checked", "outbound-fixture:re-called",
510	"dead:SendReceipt"]`. A batch in which no run takes the job to Dead fails on
511	the key, naming it, so a Dead path that the sim never exercised cannot read
512	as tested. The tail extends only for outbound work, so a pure `on_dead` job
513	whose retries outlast `tail` is bounded by `tail` as before: size `tail` to
514	its policy before you require its `dead:` key. An outbound job on the default
515	policy reaches Dead under the outage axis, which `charpente test --sim` draws
516	in a quarter of runs, half
517	of them long enough to exhaust the policy ("The outside world: remote
518	models", below), but only where its calls land inside the window. The window
519	opens in the first two seconds of virtual time, so a job called at once is
520	often answered before it opens: the fixture enqueues its receipt 2 s after the
521	order (`enqueue_after`), and measured `dead:SendReceipt` in 486 of 4096 runs,
522	against 35 of 500 when the receipt was sent at once. Measure a required key's
523	rate before you rely on it, and write the rate beside the `require`, as the
524	fixture does: a fresh `cargo test` batch is 256 runs.
525	
526	**A route the tail re-sends must be safe to receive twice.** `Drive`
527	re-sends, and a request that went unanswered may have landed, so its re-send
528	is the second delivery a production client's retry makes. Answer a repeat of
529	the same request with what the first one did, and change nothing:
530	`modelled_remote`'s `place_order` answers an order that is already stored, and
531	the scaffold's `add_note` a note already stored with the same body. A request
532	that reuses the id with other content is a
533	conflict, not a repeat: refuse it with a 4xx that names the conflict and the
534	fix, as `add_note` does for a note that already holds another body. Judge
535	the answers, not only the end state: a guard whose `==` is turned into `!=`
536	refuses the retry and answers the conflict as added, and leaves the store as
537	it was, so the scaffold's three end-state checks pass it. Its fourth,
538	`a_resent_note_changes_nothing_and_a_conflict_is_refused`, posts one note
539	twice with one body and once with another and judges each answer. Key a
540	state transition (a pickup, a cancel) by an id of its own, such as `PUT
541	/pickups/:pickup_id` naming the hold in its body and stored as a row: under
542	`POST /holds/:id/pickup` a retry of a pickup that landed and a fresh pickup of
543	a hold already picked up are the same bytes, while with its own id a repeat
544	finds its row and answers alike and a new pickup of a hold no longer waiting
545	is refused. A route
546	that fails this is an app defect the re-send found, and its check goes red
547	with a seed. Fix the route: dropping below the helper to skip the re-send
548	hides the defect.
549	
550	**Seed fixtures in the build closure, not in the phase.** A `Drive` phase is a
551	fixed request list, so a key one request mints cannot feed a later one, and
552	every setup request sent ahead of a claim's own writes pushes them later into
553	the faulted phase, where fewer get acked and more runs give up: so write the
554	fixtures (an `ApiKey` row in §5's storage form, whose raw key the requests
555	present, and the rows a claim only reads) in the closure `Drive::new` takes,
556	through `App::transact_for_tests`, each only when it is absent, since the
557	closure runs on every boot.
558	
559	`recover` gives `Ok(None)` when the run gave up by name, on a boot refused for
560	durable corruption and on nothing else. Return `Ok(())` then. Its errors fail
561	the run:
562	
563	- `the fault-free tail could not boot`: every boot met fault fallout, and
564	  nothing gave the run up.
565	- `the boot was refused for the clock a third time, after two waits past the
566	  instant each refusal named. …, so this is a platform clock defect, not the
567	  app's: report it with this run's seed. The third refusal: the fault-free tail
568	  could not boot: <refusal>`, from `wait_out_clock_refusal`. One wait always
569	  suffices, so a refusal that outlasts two is a charpente defect, and the run
570	  fails on it rather than hiding it as a skip.
571	- `the fault-free tail could not boot: <error>`: a boot, or the kernel's
572	  build, failed with an error of its own.
573	- `the fault-free tail's kernel stopped: <error>`, in the kernel's words.
574	- `the app calls <host>, but the workload registered no model for it — call
575	  sim.remote("<host>", …) before Drive::faulted_phase`, from either call.
576	- The cap: the tail ran 256 extensions, and an outbound job is still Pending
577	  and due. The text names the first such job by id:
578	
579	<!-- pinned -->
580	```text
581	Drive::recover: the tail ran 256 extensions past its horizon and outbound job <id> ("<name>") is still Pending at attempt <a> — an outbound job settles, retries to Dead, or waits for a later due time; this one did none of them within the cap of 256, so fix the model of the host it calls, or give the job, and the chain its on_dead hook makes, a retry policy that ends
582	```
583	
584	A drawn outage costs one extension however long it lasts, so the outage is
585	never what reaches the cap. A job still retrying after 256 extensions has a
586	remote that never answers it in time and a policy that has not run out (a model
587	that never answers, or a `max` in the thousands), or an `on_dead` hook that
588	starts a new link on every Dead against such a remote, so the chain never
589	ends. Fix the model, or give the job, and the chain its hook makes, a policy
590	that ends. A named job at attempt 0 was due and never dispatched, so it is a
591	row the kernel lost, not the app's: report it with the run's seed.
592	
593	- The limit: an extension has run to the year 2262, its reach meeting or
594	  passing the limit, and an outbound job is still Pending and due. The text
595	  names the job due last and its due time, and comes before the cap:
596	
597	<!-- pinned -->
598	```text
599	Drive::recover: outbound job <id> ("<name>") is still Pending at attempt <a>, due <due>, and the tail ran <n> extension<s>, the last to the year 2262, past which it does not run — a due time that far out means the job's retry backoff grew past the year 2262, so no run reaches its next attempt; give the job a retry policy that ends, a retry(max = …) small enough that it reaches Dead
600	```
601	
602	**When to drop below the helper.** `Drive` is one faulted phase and one tail.
603	A workload with more than that builds it from the pieces this section and
604	"Driving the whole app in a sim" describe: `boot_through_fallout`,
605	`Kernel::new` or `Kernel::with_outbound` over a `SimSource`, the quiesce calls
606	below and `wait_out_clock_refusal`. Examples are several faulted rounds, a
607	supervisor loop inside the phase, a script that reads one phase's answers to
608	build the next, several nodes, a check between the phase and the tail, and a
609	check that reads the frames an SSE subscriber received (`source.sinks()`):
610	`Drive` hands back neither phase's source, so it exposes no frames. §11's
611	"Testing a tail in sim" builds its source by hand to read them. A route that
612	cannot take the re-send is not a reason to drop below it: fix the route
613	(above). Keep each step's rule as `Drive` has it:
614	- use the fallout filter in every step;
615	- treat a crash in the faulted phase as the crash under test, not a skip;
616	- quiesce before the tail boots, and wait out a clock refusal;
617	- give up only on a durable refusal;
618	- re-send in the tail what went unanswered, to routes safe to receive twice.
619	
620	A check that runs at the end of a run — a checkpoint, a graceful close, a
621	byte comparison of two nodes' files — does IO, and the run's
622	`FaultConfig` still applies to it. "No fault has fired so far" is a fact about
623	the past: the check's own fsync can still draw an injected failure. Call
624	`sim.quiesce_disk_faults()` first. For the rest of the run, on every disk,
625	it disarms any pending crash countdown, and no injected read, write, sync or
626	directory-barrier error, misdirected write or restart bit flip fires after it.
627	Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it
628	replays exactly as before. After it, an error in the check is a real failure,
629	not fallout to classify. Network and object-store faults are untouched, and a
630	restart still power-cycles: unsynced writes and directory entries collapse under
631	the crash model as usual (`crash_apply`, `crash_torn`, `dir_entry_loss`).
632	
633	An outbound workload's tail needs the outbound half as well: the tail is free
634	of per-call faults, and a drawn provider outage runs to its end.
635	`sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()` ends the five outbound fault axes for the rest
636	of the run: no call started after it is refused, lost, throttled or slowed, or
637	loses its reply by chance. A drawn `outbound_outage` is not a roll and runs to
638	its own end, so calls to its host are refused after the quiesce until then.
639	Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it replays exactly
640	as before. Latency stays, since it is not a fault, and a request already in
641	flight keeps the fate it drew. Call both, then run until the outbound work
642	settles. Outside an outage's window every call reaches its remote and its
643	reply comes back, so an outbound job that is due settles or retries to Dead,
644	and inside one its calls are refused until its retries run out or the window
645	ends. `Drive::recover` runs on until then, at most 256 extensions past
646	`tail` ("The tail settles outbound work", above). A hand driver runs its tail
647	past the last backoff and deadline of every job, and of every chain its
648	`on_dead` hooks make, or loops as `recover` does. Then
649	`outbound_settles_by_horizon(snap, at)` (below) checks that every outbound job
650	due at `at`, the wall time the tail ended at, is Done or Dead, and
651	`mark_dead_coverage` marks the Dead rows' `dead:<job>` keys. A hand driver
652	reads `at` with `sim.clock().wall()` after its last run, and calls
653	`mark_dead_coverage(sim, kernel.app())` itself. Read from the clock, `at` can
654	sit below the wall the kernel holds, by up to the 60 s clock tolerance, when
655	the tail opened over a store whose recorded time was ahead of the clock (after
656	a clock refusal was waited out) and virtual time did not pass it, so a lost
657	row due in that gap passes. `Drive::recover` judges at the greater of the two.
658	
659	A realtime workload's settle phase has the same need for a different fault. The
660	subscriber-stall rate is the one fault axis the sim does not inject itself: a
661	workload reads `sim.subscriber_stall()` and drives its own sink's stall closure
662	at that rate. `sim.quiesce_subscriber_stalls()` makes that accessor read 0.0 for
663	the rest of the run, so a stall closure built after it never refuses a send
664	and draws nothing. Call it before a phase whose verdict rests on a delivery
665	completing. A stall there is a fault the property excuses, so a stall that drops
666	the only clean attempt's tail leaves the run with no verdict at all.
667	
668	A tail that opens a kernel needs the clock half too.
669	`sim.quiesce_clock_faults()` ends the clock faults ("Wall time and its faults",
670	below) for the rest of the run, on every clock. No reading steps back and
671	no power cycle jumps a clock forward after it, so each clock's offset stays
672	where the run left it, skew included. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a
673	run that never calls it replays exactly as before. It does not undo the
674	past: a step back in an earlier phase can leave the clock more than the
675	tolerance behind the latest time the store recorded, and then the tail's open is
676	refused (§7). With the offset frozen, the clock reaches the instant the refusal
677	names as virtual time passes. `clock_reopens_after(text)` (below) reads that
678	instant. Sleep a little past it (`sim.clock().sleep(…)`), restart the process (a
679	refused node exits, and its supervisor starts it again), and boot again. One
680	wait is enough, since nothing moves the clock or the recorded time in between.
681	Bound the loop anyway, and fail the run by name once the bound is spent: no
682	injected fault explains a refusal one wait did not clear, so it is a platform
683	defect, and a skip would hide it. `wait_out_clock_refusal(sim, boot)` (below)
684	is that loop, and `Drive::recover` runs it around the tail's boot.
685	
686	### Restarting the process, not the machine
687	
688	`sim.restart()` is a power cycle: every unsynced write survives, tears or
689	vanishes before anything reopens. Most restarts in production are not that. A
690	supervisor restarting a crashed, killed or exited process finds the OS page
691	cache intact: every write the dead process made is still readable, synced or
692	not. `sim.restart_process()` models that. Every open file handle dies, exactly
693	as after `restart`, and nothing else happens. Unsynced writes and directory
694	entries stay pending and readable, and the next `restart()` still collapses
695	them.
696	
697	The difference matters because readable is not durable. A node that reads back
698	what a dead process wrote and persists anything derived from it, before making
699	it durable, has built on data the next power loss can take away. A store
700	outran its own log exactly that way: recovery replayed a WAL frame whose fsync
701	had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
702

A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:

| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
|---|---|---|
| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |

Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it

offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
